title: Honey Face Mask Base
description: Signature edition: an original Signature design in the same family. A honey face mask base is a ready-to-use cosmetic base: honey blended with clay or oat flour into a smooth paste that is spread on the face, left for a short time, and rinsed off. Honey acts in the base as a humectant, drawing moisture to the skin, and as the paste body. Traditional use of honey on skin is evidence-graded as mixed: honey is a well-known humectant and its moisturizing feel is supported, while stronger skin claims are traditional and unproven, and this record makes no stronger claim. The honey-uses skincare record covers the traditional method of honey skin care; this record covers the mask base as a formulated product, with its grades and batch figures. This is an original design, not a historical public record.
instructions: Mix honey with clay or oat flour in the ratio given in the demo until the paste is smooth and spreadable.
Stir in a few drops of plant oil if the grade calls for it, and jar the base at once.
Patch-test the base on a small area of skin and wait a day before full use.
Spread a thin layer on clean skin, leave it for 10 to 15 minutes, and rinse with lukewarm water.
Label the jar with ingredients, date, and the instruction to discard the base if it smells off or changes color.
safety: Skin-contact note: this product is not food. Patch-test on a small area of skin first, stop using it if irritation appears, keep it out of eyes, and do not use it on broken skin. Traditional cosmetic uses of honey are evidence-graded in the description (supported, mixed, or traditional and unproven) and are never presented as healing or medical products. Made without any slaughter-derived ingredient; plant oils, plant butters, and plant waxes are used. Mask bases with no preservative keep only a short time and must be kept cool; discard any base that ferments, smells sour, or grows mold. Never share jars or applicators.
variations: Clay mask base for oily-feeling skin.
Oat mask base for dry-feeling skin.
yield: A 300 g batch of mask base fills 5 jars; see the demo.

title: Honey Cosmetic Preservation and Shelf-Life System
description: Signature edition: an original Signature design in the same family. The honey cosmetic preservation and shelf-life system is the specification for keeping honey cosmetics safe: water activity figures, preservative choices, packaging, storage temperatures, and discard rules for every honey cosmetic product type. Honey itself resists microbes at low water activity, but once honey is diluted into creams, serums, and soaps, the water activity rises and preservation becomes essential. This record gives the system tables and the batch-testing figures. It is a safety and formulation system, not a product for sale on its own, and it makes no medical claim of any kind. This record partially supersedes the later-wave honey-skincare pair for the preservation side, which will need re-mapping. This is an original design, not a historical public record.
materials: Preservatives suited to each product type
instructions: Measure water activity for each honey cosmetic type and record it in the system table.
Choose a preservative suited to each type and test it at the maker's recommended level.
Pack test batches in sterilized packaging and store them at room temperature and in warmth.
Check the test batches weekly for smell, color, separation, and growth, and record the results.
Write the shelf-life and discard rule for each type from the test results, and print it on every label.
safety: Skin-contact note: this product is not food. Patch-test on a small area of skin first, stop using it if irritation appears, keep it out of eyes, and do not use it on broken skin. Traditional cosmetic uses of honey are evidence-graded in the description (supported, mixed, or traditional and unproven) and are never presented as healing or medical products. Preservation rules are safety rules: any honey cosmetic that smells sour, ferments, separates badly, or grows mold is discarded, never sold or shared.
